title: Study of Compounds: Sulphuric Acid
tagline: Understand the manufacture, properties and uses of sulphuric acid.

overview.intro: Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) is a vital industrial chemical often called the king of chemicals due to its wide applications. It is manufactured by the Contact process and exhibits properties of a strong acid, a dehydrating agent and, in concentrated form, an oxidising agent. This chapter covers manufacture, physical and chemical properties, important reactions, tests for sulphates and safe handling practices relevant to ICSE study.

learningOutcomes: Outline the Contact process for manufacture of sulphuric acid with key conditions.
Describe physical properties and safe dilution of concentrated sulphuric acid.
Explain acidic, dehydrating and oxidising properties with examples.
Write equations for important reactions with metals, salts and organic substances.
Identify tests for sulphuric acid and sulphate ions.

blocks.text: Sulphuric acid is manufactured industrially by the Contact process. Sulphur or sulphide ores are burned to produce sulphur dioxide (SO2), which is purified and then oxidised to sulphur trioxide (SO3) by oxygen in presence of a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at about 450°C and 1–2 atm pressure: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3.

Sulphur trioxide is not absorbed directly in water because it forms a dense fog of sulphuric acid. Instead, it is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum (H2S2O7), which is then carefully diluted with water to obtain sulphuric acid of desired concentration: SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7; H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4.

items: Purification of gases prevents catalyst poisoning.
Moderate temperature favours good yield with reasonable rate.
Excess air/oxygen drives oxidation of SO2 to SO3.
Absorption in concentrated acid avoids acid mist formation.

blocks.text: Concentrated sulphuric acid is a colourless, oily, dense liquid. It is highly hygroscopic and has strong affinity for water, releasing a large amount of heat when mixed with water. For this reason, acid must always be added slowly to water with stirring, never water to acid, to prevent splashing and accidents.

As a dibasic acid, sulphuric acid can form two series of salts: normal sulphates and acid sulphates (hydrogen sulphates). Its high boiling point and non-volatile nature allow it to displace more volatile acids from their salts, a property used in laboratory preparations.

items.meaning: Fuming sulphuric acid formed by dissolving SO3 in concentrated H2SO4.
Readily absorbing moisture from the surroundings.
An acid that can produce two replaceable hydrogen ions per molecule.

blocks.text: Dilute sulphuric acid behaves as a typical strong acid. It reacts with active metals to produce hydrogen gas, with bases to form salt and water, and with carbonates or bicarbonates to release carbon dioxide. These reactions produce sulphates (or hydrogen sulphates) depending on conditions.

Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a powerful dehydrating agent, removing elements of water from compounds. It chars sugar and paper by removing hydrogen and oxygen as water, leaving carbon, and dehydrates substances such as hydrated copper(II) sulphate (turning blue crystals white) and formic/oxalic acids in specific reactions.

items.note: Dehydration leaves a black mass of carbon.
Concentrated acid removes water of crystallisation.

blocks.text: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidising agent. It oxidises metals such as copper (which do not react with dilute acids to liberate hydrogen) to form metal sulphates, while being reduced to sulphur dioxide. It can also oxidise non-metals like carbon and sulphur under suitable conditions.

As a non-volatile acid, concentrated sulphuric acid is used to prepare volatile acids such as HCl and HNO3 from their salts. In such reactions, it displaces the more volatile acid on heating. Care must be taken to distinguish these displacement reactions from redox behaviour.

Sulphate ions in solution are tested by adding barium chloride solution in presence of dilute hydrochloric acid, producing a white precipitate of barium sulphate insoluble in acids. This test is characteristic of sulphates and dilute sulphuric acid. Concentrated sulphuric acid can also be identified by its dehydrating action and other reactions.

Sulphuric acid is used in fertilizers, batteries, detergents, dyes, explosives and petroleum refining. Because of its corrosive and dehydrating nature, concentrated acid must be handled with protective equipment, and dilution must always be done by adding acid to water slowly with stirring.

items: Add acid to water, never water to acid.
Barium chloride gives white BaSO4 precipitate with sulphates.
Concentrated acid can cause severe burns and charring of organic matter.
Store in appropriate containers away from incompatible substances.

keyPoints: Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the Contact process using catalytic oxidation of SO2 to SO3.
SO3 is absorbed in concentrated H2SO4 to form oleum, then diluted to give H2SO4.
Concentrated sulphuric acid is dense, oily, hygroscopic and a strong dehydrating agent.
Always add acid to water slowly when diluting to avoid splashing and heat hazards.
Dilute sulphuric acid shows typical acid reactions forming sulphates and hydrogen with active metals.
Hot concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidising agent, producing SO2 in many reactions.
Sulphate ions give a white precipitate of BaSO4 with barium chloride in dilute HCl.
Concentrated H2SO4 can displace volatile acids from their salts due to non-volatility.
Dehydration removes elements of water, charring carbohydrates and organic matter.
Correct conditions (dilute vs concentrated, hot vs cold) determine reaction products.

questions.prompt: Sulphuric acid is manufactured industrially by the:
questions.answer: Contact process
questions.explanation: The Contact process produces sulphuric acid by catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide.
questions.commonMistake: Ostwald process is used for nitric acid.

questions.prompt: When diluting concentrated sulphuric acid, one should:
options: add acid to water slowly with stirring
questions.answer: add acid to water slowly with stirring
questions.explanation: Adding acid to water dissipates heat safely and prevents splashing of corrosive acid.
questions.commonMistake: Adding water to concentrated acid can cause violent spurting.

questions.prompt: In the Contact process, the catalyst used is:
questions.answer: vanadium(V) oxide
questions.explanation: V2O5 catalyses the oxidation of SO2 to SO3 efficiently.
questions.commonMistake: Platinum-rhodium is used in the Ostwald process.

questions.prompt: Concentrated sulphuric acid chars sugar because it acts as a:
questions.answer: dehydrating agent
questions.explanation: It removes elements of water from sugar, leaving behind carbon.
questions.commonMistake: Charring is due to dehydration, not simple burning in air.

questions.prompt: A white precipitate insoluble in dilute HCl formed with BaCl2 indicates:
questions.answer: sulphate ions
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate is an insoluble white precipitate characteristic of sulphates.
questions.commonMistake: Acidification prevents confusion with some other precipitates.

questions.prompt: Oleum is formed when SO3 is absorbed in:
questions.answer: concentrated sulphuric acid
questions.explanation: Absorption in concentrated acid avoids formation of acid mist and produces oleum.
questions.commonMistake: Direct absorption of SO3 in water is not used industrially.

questions.prompt: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with copper to produce:
questions.answer: sulphur dioxide gas
questions.explanation: Concentrated acid acts as an oxidising agent, being reduced to SO2 while oxidising copper.
questions.commonMistake: Copper does not liberate hydrogen with dilute non-oxidising acids.

questions.prompt: Sulphuric acid can displace HCl from NaCl because it is:
questions.answer: non-volatile
questions.explanation: A non-volatile acid can displace a more volatile acid from its salt on heating.
questions.commonMistake: This is a displacement based on volatility, not just acid strength.

questions.prompt: Sulphuric acid is a ________ acid because it has two replaceable hydrogen atoms.
questions.answer: dibasic
questions.explanation: Dibasic acids can form normal and acid salts.
questions.commonMistake: Monobasic acids like HCl have one replaceable hydrogen.

questions.prompt: In the Contact process, sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to form ________.
questions.answer: oleum
questions.explanation: Oleum is later diluted with water to obtain sulphuric acid.
questions.commonMistake: Direct absorption in water creates acid mist.

questions.prompt: The white precipitate formed with barium chloride and a sulphate is barium ________.
questions.answer: sulphate
questions.explanation: BaSO4 is insoluble and confirms presence of sulphate ions.
questions.commonMistake: Ensure the test is done in presence of dilute HCl to avoid interference.

questions.prompt: State the catalyst and temperature used in the Contact process.
questions.answer: Vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) is used as the catalyst at about 450°C in the Contact process.
questions.explanation: These conditions provide a good balance between rate and yield.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse with catalysts used in other industrial processes.

questions.prompt: Why is sulphur trioxide not absorbed directly in water in the Contact process?
questions.answer: Sulphur trioxide reacts vigorously with water to form a dense fog of sulphuric acid mist, which is difficult to condense. Therefore it is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum, which is then diluted safely.
questions.explanation: Industrial absorption avoids loss and handling problems caused by acid mist.
questions.commonMistake: State the practical problem (acid mist/fog) clearly.

questions.prompt: Explain the dehydrating action of concentrated sulphuric acid with the example of sugar.
questions.answer: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes the elements of water (hydrogen and oxygen in 2:1 ratio) from sugar. This leaves behind a black, porous mass of carbon while water is released, showing strong dehydrating action: C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O in presence of conc. H2SO4.
questions.explanation: The black residue is carbon formed after removal of water elements.
questions.commonMistake: Dehydration is different from drying by simple absorption of free water.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for the reaction of hot concentrated sulphuric acid with copper and state the observation.
questions.answer: Cu + 2H2SO4(conc., hot) → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O. Brown copper reacts to form a blue solution of copper sulphate and sulphur dioxide gas with a pungent smell is evolved.
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidising agent in this reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Include conditions (hot, concentrated) for this reaction.

questions.prompt: Describe the main steps of the Contact process for manufacture of sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Sulphur dioxide is produced by burning sulphur or roasting sulphide ores and is purified. The purified SO2 is mixed with excess air and passed over vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at about 450°C to form sulphur trioxide: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3. Sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum (H2S2O7), which is then diluted with water to obtain sulphuric acid of required concentration.
questions.explanation: The process avoids direct absorption of SO3 in water and uses catalytic oxidation.
questions.commonMistake: Mention purification and oleum formation as key steps.

questions.prompt: Compare the action of dilute and concentrated sulphuric acid on (i) zinc and (ii) copper.
questions.answer: (i) Dilute sulphuric acid reacts with zinc to produce zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas: Zn + H2SO4(dil.) → ZnSO4 + H2. Concentrated sulphuric acid, especially when hot, can act as an oxidising agent, but the typical acid-metal hydrogen reaction is characteristic of dilute acid with active metals. (ii) Copper does not react with dilute sulphuric acid to liberate hydrogen. Hot concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with copper to form copper sulphate, sulphur dioxide and water: Cu + 2H2SO4(conc.) → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O.
questions.explanation: Metal reactivity and acid concentration determine whether hydrogen or SO2 is produced.
questions.commonMistake: State conditions clearly; copper needs hot concentrated acid.

questions.prompt: Explain three different chemical roles of sulphuric acid with one example each.
questions.answer: (1) As an acid (dilute): reacts with metals like zinc to form zinc sulphate and hydrogen, Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2. (2) As a dehydrating agent (concentrated): removes elements of water from sugar, leaving carbon, C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O. (3) As an oxidising agent (hot concentrated): oxidises copper to copper sulphate with evolution of sulphur dioxide, Cu + 2H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O. These roles depend on concentration and conditions.
questions.explanation: Examples should clearly illustrate each distinct role.
questions.commonMistake: Specify dilute or concentrated/hot conditions for each role.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish between dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulphuric acid using barium chloride solution?
questions.answer: Add barium chloride solution to each acid. With dilute sulphuric acid, a white precipitate of barium sulphate forms immediately: BaCl2 + H2SO4 → BaSO4↓ + 2HCl. With dilute hydrochloric acid, no white precipitate is formed because barium chloride is soluble. The formation of insoluble white BaSO4 identifies sulphuric acid.
questions.explanation: The sulphate ion gives a characteristic precipitate with barium ions.
questions.commonMistake: Ensure reagents are correctly identified; barium chloride is the test solution.

questions.prompt: A student adds water to concentrated sulphuric acid and the mixture splashes. Explain why this happened and state the correct procedure.
questions.answer: Dilution of concentrated sulphuric acid is highly exothermic. Adding water to acid causes the small amount of water to heat rapidly, boil and splatter, carrying corrosive acid. The correct procedure is to add concentrated acid slowly to water with constant stirring so that the larger volume of water absorbs the heat safely.
questions.explanation: Heat dissipation and prevention of splashing depend on the order of mixing.
questions.commonMistake: Always remember: acid to water, never water to acid.

questions.prompt: Blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulphate turn white when left in concentrated sulphuric acid. Explain the observation and identify the property involved.
questions.answer: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4·5H2O) is blue due to water of crystallisation. Concentrated sulphuric acid has a strong affinity for water and acts as a dehydrating agent, removing the water of crystallisation from the crystals. This forms anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, which is white: CuSO4·5H2O → CuSO4 + 5H2O. The colour change demonstrates the dehydrating property of concentrated sulphuric acid.
questions.explanation: Loss of water of crystallisation changes both composition and colour.
questions.commonMistake: Distinguish dehydration of crystals from dissolving the salt.

questions.prompt: Why can concentrated sulphuric acid be used to prepare hydrogen chloride from sodium chloride, but not to prepare hydrogen bromide from sodium bromide in the same simple way?
questions.answer: Concentrated sulphuric acid is non-volatile and can displace volatile HCl from NaCl. However, hot concentrated sulphuric acid is also an oxidising agent and oxidises hydrogen bromide (and iodide) to bromine (or iodine), so pure HBr cannot be obtained by this method. Thus, while volatility allows displacement, the oxidising nature of concentrated H2SO4 interferes with HBr preparation.
questions.explanation: Both non-volatility and oxidising behaviour must be considered for different halides.
questions.commonMistake: Consider secondary reactions caused by oxidising concentrated sulphuric acid.
